title: The relative pin

card.idea: When the piece behind is not the king but something valuable, the piece in front is allowed to move. It just costs you. That is a relative pin, and it is a chain rather than a wall: strong enough that nobody wants to break it, but it can be broken.

explain.text: White's queen on d1 looks up the d-file. The knight on d7 is in the way and the black queen sits behind it on d8. The knight may move — nothing in the rules stops it — but the moment it does, the queens are looking at each other and Black's comes off.

So treat it like a stuck piece. The white knight has come to e5 and attacks d7 a second time. Black may still play the knight away, but then he is handing over a queen to save a knight, which nobody does.
The piece behind does not have to be a queen. Here the knight on d5 shields a rook, so moving it costs the exchange. A pawn coming to e4 is enough to win it.

challenges.prompt: The knight on d7 is allowed to move. So why would Black rather not move it?
options: The white queen on d1 would then take the black queen on d8.
The knight would be taken by the knight on f3.
It would put the black king in check.

hints.text: Cover the knight on d7 with your thumb and look at what is left on the d-file.

challenges.reason: Queen on d1, knight on d7, queen on d8. Take the knight out of the middle and the two queens meet.

challenges.prompt: Tap the square your knight on f3 goes to so that it also attacks the knight on d7.

hints.text: A knight on e5 reaches c4, c6, d3, d7, f7, g6, g4 and f3.

challenges.reason: e5 is the only square the knight on f3 can reach that touches d7.

challenges.prompt: White plays the knight to e5, where the knight on d7 can reach it. Is the white knight safe there?
reasons: No. The knight on d7 simply takes it and wins a piece.
Yes, for all practical purposes. Nxe5 is legal, but then Qxd8 wins the black queen.
No. The pawn on f7 takes it.

hints.text: Ask what Black would have to give up to make the capture.

challenges.reason: This is the difference from a pin against the king: the capture is legal here, it is just far too expensive.

challenges.prompt: The knight on d7 is not going anywhere. Bring a second attacker to it.

wrong.Qxd7: You take a knight and Black takes your queen back. The pin was doing the work; do not trade it for one piece.

challenges.reason: Ne5 attacks d7 twice over. Black cannot defend it again, and moving it costs the queen.

challenges.prompt: Tap the black piece that the knight on d5 is standing in front of.

hints.text: Follow the d-file up from the white rook and keep going past the knight.

challenges.reason: The rook on d8. That is what makes the knight on d5 reluctant to move.

challenges.prompt: Attack the knight on d5 with a pawn.

wrong.Rxd5: The rook takes a knight and the rook on d8 takes back. You have given five points for three.

challenges.reason: e4 hits the knight. Moving it hands over the rook on d8, so Black loses material either way.

challenges.prompt: How is this different from a piece pinned in front of its own king?
options: This knight is allowed to move. It simply costs the rook behind it.
This knight is not allowed to move either.
There is no difference at all.

hints.text: One kind of pin is a rule. The other is a price.

challenges.reason: Only a king makes a pin absolute. Everything else is a price, and a desperate opponent will pay it.

takeaway: A piece pinned to something valuable may legally move — it just costs. Attack it again and make the price impossible.
